The alfonsino (Beryx decadactylus) is a moderately large, deep-water beryciform fish with a notably slow life history. Juveniles and sub-adults inhabit the mesopelagic zone over continental slopes, gradually migrating to deeper waters as they mature. Field surveys suggest that the ultimate total length attained by this species reaches 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], which is among the largest recorded for its family. This considerable body size is accompanied by an extended juvenile phase, during which individuals remain pre-reproductive and slowly accumulate somatic mass. Early life stages are particularly vulnerable; based on the egg diameter of approximately 1.1 millimeters observed in the congeneric Beryx splendens, the wet weight at birth for an alfonsino is estimated to be 0.0007 grams [Wwb = 0.0007 grams]. This minute starting mass reflects the pelagic, yolk-dependent nature of the newly emerged prolarva. The period from hatching to the onset of exogenous feeding is critical, with the lecithotrophic larva relying entirely on its yolk reserves before the trophic switch occurs. Comparative data from related berycids indicate that egg size is a strong predictor of larval survival under variable oceanic conditions, making this initial mass a key parameter in understanding recruitment dynamics.

The onset of gonadal maturation in alfonsino does not occur until individuals have achieved a substantial body size. Stock assessments and histological analyses of gonad tissue indicate that the total length at puberty is approximately 27.6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 27.6 centimeters]. This length marks the transition from an immature, growing juvenile to a sexually maturing teleost capable of initiating gametogenesis. The delay in reaching this developmental milestone is consistent with the species' overall slow-growth strategy, which is typical of many deep-water fishes that experience low natural mortality and relatively stable, oligotrophic environments. Puberty itself represents the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, after which vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis commence in females and males, respectively. This size threshold is an important reference for fisheries management, as it indicates the minimum length at which individuals can contribute to the breeding population. Below this size, all captured specimens are immature and have not yet participated in reproduction, making the Lp value a crucial parameter for setting size limits and evaluating the reproductive potential of the stock under exploitation.

Under the stable, cold thermal regime typical of the alfonsino's deep-water habitat, approximately 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C], the species exhibits a remarkably extended lifespan. Tagging studies and otolith age readings have documented a maximum longevity of 69 years [am = 69 years], placing Beryx decadactylus among the longest-lived teleosts known at a temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C]. This extreme lifespan is characteristic of slow-growing, late-maturing deep-sea fishes and is closely tied to the low metabolic costs of living in cold, hypoxic waters. Senescence in this species appears to be a gradual process, with post-reproductive adults showing no sudden physiological decline. This life-history trait makes the alfonsino particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as the population's turnover rate is exceedingly slow and recovery from depletion can take many decades or even centuries. The 69-year lifespan stands in stark contrast to the short-lived, fast-growing epipelagic species that inhabit warmer surface waters.

The maximum reproductive rate of Beryx decadactylus has been estimated based on allometric scaling from the closely related Beryx splendens. At a constant water temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C], a 100-centimeter female alfonsino can produce approximately 5370 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 5370 eggs per day], a value derived from the scaling relationship of fecundity with body mass. This high daily fecundity reflects the enormous energetic investment that a large, iteroparous female can direct toward offspring production. The eggs are pelagic and small, as inferred from the congeneric birth mass of 0.0007 grams [Wwb = 0.0007 grams], which produces a large number of offspring per unit of maternal investment. The combination of late maturity, extreme longevity, and high fecundity aligns with a bet-hedging strategy typical of fishes that experience highly variable recruitment success in the deep ocean.

As individuals approach their maximum size, the allometric relationship between length and mass becomes evident. The ultimate wet weight of a 100-centimeter alfonsino is calculated to be approximately 18,100 grams [Wwi = approximately 18,100 grams], based on a length-weight relationship typical for berycids. This substantial mass is composed largely of muscle tissue and lipid stores, which are essential for buoyancy control and energy reserves during the long non-feeding periods that can occur in deep-water environments. The growth trajectory slows markedly after the attainment of puberty at 27.6 centimeters [Lp = 27.6 centimeters], with most somatic growth occurring in the first half of the lifespan. Comparative physiological studies suggest that the maximum wet weight of approximately 18,100 grams [Wwi = approximately 18,100 grams] is close to the theoretical upper limit imposed by the species' metabolic capacity and the oxygen availability in its cold habitat at 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C]. Overall, the life history of Beryx decadactylus is characterized by a slow pace of life, with late maturation, high fecundity, and exceptional longevity, all traits that make it highly sensitive to anthropogenic mortality.
